title: Namespaces
relevance: Interviewers probe whether candidates prevent name collisions, use using-declarations vs directives safely (especially in headers), and understand ADL and linkage rules in real C++ codebases.

phases.goal: Establish why namespaces exist and how they are defined and accessed.

must_hit.point: Namespaces group related names into a distinct declarative scope to prevent name collisions across libraries and large projects.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions two libraries both defining Socket and how namespaces avoid the compilation error.

must_hit.point: Namespaces are open: the same namespace can be reopened and extended across multiple files or blocks.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes Graphics in graphics_engine.h and reopening Graphics in graphics_renderer.h to add renderFrame.

must_hit.point: Names outside a namespace are accessed with the scope-resolution operator ::.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives an example like Graphics::Window myWindow.

probes: Why do we need namespaces, and how do you access a name defined inside one?

hints.1: Think about two third-party libraries defining the same class name.
hints.2: Cover the namespace keyword, that namespaces can be reopened, and how :: qualifies a name.
hints.3: Say namespaces are open declarative regions; access members with Namespace::Name, e.g. Graphics::Window.

phases.goal: Cover nested namespaces, aliases, using forms, anonymous namespaces, ADL, std rules, and inline namespaces.

must_hit.point: Namespaces nest hierarchically; C++17 allows compact nested syntax like namespace Engine::Physics::Collision.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts pre-C++17 nested opens with the Engine::Physics::Collision compact form and fully qualified calls.

must_hit.point: A namespace alias shortens a long path, e.g. namespace EPC = Engine::Physics::Collision.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Compares it to Python import ... as plt and shows EPC::checkIntersection().

must_hit.point: A using-declaration imports exactly one name; a using-directive imports all names from a namespace.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts using std::cout with using namespace std and notes endl is not imported by the declaration alone.

must_hit.point: Names in an anonymous namespace have internal linkage and are visible only in that translation unit.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States they are the modern preferred replacement for file-scope static on variables or free functions.

must_hit.point: ADL (Koenig lookup) adds the namespaces of a call’s argument types to the scopes searched for an unqualified function.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains std::cout << name finding std::operator<< because ostream and string live in std.

must_hit.point: You must not add your own declarations to namespace std (undefined behaviour), except specializing standard templates for your types.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Cites specializing std::hash for a user-defined User type as the allowed exception.

must_hit.point: C++11 inline namespaces expose members as if they were in the parent namespace, commonly for library versioning.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Shows MyLib::doWork() resolving to inline v2 while MyLib::v1::doWork() remains explicit.

probes: What is the difference between using std::cout; and using namespace std;?
What is ADL, and why does std::cout << name work without qualifying operator<<?
What is an anonymous namespace, and how does it relate to internal linkage?

hints.1: Separate importing one name from importing an entire namespace, then think about lookup and linkage.
hints.2: Walk through using-declaration vs directive, unnamed namespaces, ADL on argument namespaces, and inline versioning.
hints.3: using-declaration is surgical; using-directive dumps all names; anonymous namespaces give internal linkage; ADL searches argument namespaces; do not open std except for allowed specializations; inline namespaces surface as parent members.

phases.goal: Judge when to fully qualify, alias, surgically using-declare, or locally using-direct.

must_hit.point: Prefer using-declarations over using-directives because directives are blunt and invite naming ambiguities.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Notes std is massive and global using namespace std defeats namespaces and can clash with names like data or size.

must_hit.point: If a using-directive is needed, restrict it to a function or local block rather than file/global scope.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says professional practice keeps using namespace std out of global/file scope and limits it locally when used.

must_hit.point: Anonymous namespaces are preferred over legacy file-scope static for hiding translation-unit-local names.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Calls anonymous namespaces the modern preferred C++ replacement for static on file-scope variables or free functions.

probes: When would you choose a using-declaration over a using-directive, and where is each acceptable?

hints.1: Ask what gets imported and how wide the scope is.
hints.2: Compare surgical one-name import vs whole-namespace import, and global vs function-local placement.
hints.3: Prefer using std::cout; avoid global using namespace std; if needed, put the directive inside a function; prefer anonymous namespaces over file-scope static.

phases.goal: Apply namespace rules to headers, the standard library, and versioned library APIs.

must_hit.point: Never put a using-directive such as using namespace std; in a header file.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains every includer silently imports the whole namespace and will hit collisions.

must_hit.point: Library authors can use inline namespaces so clients call MyLib::doWork() while older versions remain reachable as MyLib::v1::doWork().
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes shipping updates without breaking clients that rely on unqualified parent-namespace names.

must_hit.point: The only valid reason shown to open namespace std is template specialization for a user-defined type.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Walks through specializing std::hash<User> and states adding other declarations to std is undefined behaviour.

probes: Why is using namespace std; especially bad in a header?
How would you version a library API with namespaces so old and new clients both work?

hints.1: Think about what happens to every file that #includes you.
hints.2: Connect header pollution to collisions, and inline nested namespaces to default vs explicit versions.
hints.3: Header using-directives force the whole namespace on consumers; inline v2 makes MyLib::doWork map to the new API while MyLib::v1 stays available; only specialize std templates, do not add arbitrary names to std.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: A using-declaration imports one name surgically (e.g. using std::cout;); a using-directive imports every name from the namespace. Directives at global scope, especially using namespace std;, defeat namespaces and invite ambiguities; if used at all, keep them inside a function or local block.

Anonymous (unnamed) namespaces give internal linkage so names are local to the translation unit and will not collide with same names in other TUs; they are the modern preferred replacement for applying static to file-scope variables or free functions.

gotchas.trap: Placing using namespace std; (or any using-directive) in a header or at global/file scope.
gotchas.correction: Never put using-directives in headers; avoid them globally. Prefer fully qualified names or using-declarations; if a directive is needed, confine it to a function or local block.

gotchas.trap: Adding your own declarations or definitions to namespace std.
gotchas.correction: That is undefined behaviour. The permitted exception is specializing standard templates (e.g. std::hash) for your own types.

gotchas.trap: Assuming std::cout << name requires an explicit std::operator<< qualification.
gotchas.correction: ADL (Koenig lookup) searches the namespaces of the argument types (here std for ostream and string), so the matching operator<< is found without explicit qualification.
